coherence.reasons: X's governing thought breaks into four pillars (worth ~$2M not $8M; Pro tier with allowance; mobile first, Q4 launch; validate with a trigger), and each slide title supports one of them. The five-condition test of the CPO's plan on slide 3 sets up the rest of the deck. Its one tension, that Copilot is needed for NRR yet delayed, is addressed directly through the 2028 migration-timing argument. Y's hierarchy is also orderly, but it has internal strains. It says to launch on the productivity case while showing that case is proven only among volunteers. Its sequencing pages show mobile-first loses less lasting ARR above a 34% fix rate, yet it concludes Copilot first. Its Q1 test is said to 'decide' between Pro and the add-on, and a missed productivity threshold to 'delay launch', although the Q2 launch and engineering commitment are already approved.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend a Pro tier at +$12 per seat with a usage allowance and reject the $149 add-on and free inclusion, so both meet the defensibility criteria. They differ on timing. X puts mobile first and launches in Q4 2027, which is the key's conditional option; it meets the conditions by quantifying the win-rate risk (~$0.32M per half-year), planning a limited AI response (beta kept live, early access in Routewise deals) and setting a mid-February trigger with break-even thresholds. It weighs both delays in the same terms, runs a sensitivity grid, and admits 'the money is close' before naming its tie-breakers. Y accepts the mobile delay explicitly, which is also defensible, but weighs it less well. Its own numbers favour mobile-first on lasting ARR, and the deciding argument (only Pro is sized for the NRR target) ignores that lower mobile churn also lifts NRR, which Y never sizes. Y's base case also leans on 33% take-up from a single precedent, where X uses a discounted 25% with a 14–33% range.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core calculations right: $8.06M vs $2.45M, inference of $32.4 / $61.2 / $130.5 per account, and 109 deals worth $0.64M. Both flag the volunteer bias, the survey's 6% response and size skew, the Routewise discount confound, and that a loss-note mention is not a cause. Y's Pro economics match the key exactly ($2.89M ARR, $1.26M inference, 76.0% company margin). X instead assumes usage scales per seat (444 per seat), which gives a lower inference cost and a 67% contribution margin; that assumption is stated but not supported, though X also runs a heavy-user case. X goes further in three places: it shows the Sales memo implies a 58% win rate, above the 44% before Routewise's change; it catches that Table 2 implies the top 10% generate ~40% of requests, not the stated 58%; and it sizes mobile's NRR effect. X also relies on several 50% midpoint assumptions, all labelled, where Y uses upper bounds. Y rests its launch case on productivity evidence it concedes is biased, and shows $0.01 per request in one backup table. On balance X is slightly ahead.

revision.reasons: Both keep 'launch' and revise the packaging and the $8M sizing using the paywall test and the inference cost, which is the expected handling. X tests the CPO's hypothesis as five necessary conditions, gives a verdict on each, and replaces the $8M with a range of $1.2–2.9M; it also revises timing with the mobile trade-off made explicit. Y has a clear from-to page covering five changes, but its replacement revenue case is the single figure of $2.9M at 33% take-up, the optimistic end, although flagged for testing. X's revision is somewhat more rigorous and better calibrated.

overall.reasons: Both documents avoid the traps and reach defensible conclusions with the same packaging. X would serve the CEO better because it sizes Copilot and mobile in the same ARR and NRR terms, shows how sensitive the sequencing call is, and gives explicit triggers and gates for bringing the launch forward. It also keeps a limited AI response in place during the delay and uses more conservative base cases. Y is sound on the numbers and matches the key's Pro economics more closely, but its Q2 launch call sits uneasily with its own delay analysis, depends on 33% take-up, and its pre-launch tests cannot really gate a launch that is already committed.
